newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech Jan output tumbles, analysts wary of trend.
newsitem.headline: Czech Jan output tumbles, analysts wary of trend.

text.p: The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) said on Wednesday construction and industrial output tumbled in January while wages continued to rise, blaming the poor figures on seasonal factors and a change in methodology.

The CSU said real industrial output in January contracted by 3.9 percent, year-on-year, while average industrial monthly wages grew, in nominal terms, 14.4 percent and construction output fell 18.6 percent, year-on-year.

Analysts said they were disappointed by the figures, and that CSU explanations that poor winter weather conditions, changes to its methodology and bloated figures due to the construction of the Ingolstadt pipeline last year did not tell the whole story.

"It's disappointing. Part of the reason can be explained by methodological and seasonl factors but I have suspicions that these cannot explain the whole situation," Martin Kupka, an economist at Patria Finance told Reuters.
"But we have to wait two or three months to verify these suspicions," he added.

The CSU said the new methodology for industrial production excludes multiple calculation of semi-finished products, resources, and other materials and commodities, which were included in output data at every stage under the old method measuring the gross value of all goods produced.
The new index measures output changes by units, weight or other measurements, of the total of 1,304 products out of 879 product groups consisting of one or more similar products.

The product groups's output indices are placed in sectors, using weighting equal to their weight in the respective industrial sector. The overall index is calculated from weighted changes in the sectoral indices.
With regard to construction output, the CSU said a cold snap this winter helped cut the average number of working hours by some 10.6 percent, year-on-year in January.
It added the year-on-year figure was also influenced by a rush of construction in January 1996 on the Ingolstadt oil pipeline.
"The construction figures are almost 20 percent lower and this seems to be a very bad result," said one analyst.
"When the CSU argues that the number of working hours was 10 percent lower, I would expect the figure to be about 10 percent lower, but it is almost double this," he added.

Added Kupka: "I am not sure about the argument concerning Ingolstadt because according to my figures construction growth was about six percent in January 1996 and the year before it was almost the same, and not an exceptionally strong base."
Analysts also said wage growth continues to be a concern, especially after Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus predicted on Tuesday that the economy was growing slower than expected.
They said that given the slowing economy and contracting output, wage growth must slow as well or inflation will accelerate.
